attempts.rationale: The series has a strong trend (trend_strength=0.83) and unstable model rankings (ranking_tau=0.15), which suggests that robust aggregation methods like median or trimmed mean are likely to outperform simple average or inverse-error weighting, as they are less sensitive to outliers and ranking shifts. I will start by testing the Median combination over the full pool to establish a robust baseline.

The ranking stability is extremely low (tau=0.15) and unstable across windows, which favors robust aggregation over error-weighting. Since simple median and trimmed mean are leading, I will test DBA (Distribution-Based Agreement), a robust method that relies on consensus rather than pointwise errors, to see if it captures the underlying signal better in this high-uncertainty regime.

A trimmed mean on the full pool is a strong candidate that balances accuracy and robustness.

The ranking instability (tau=0.15) and trend-dominated regime suggest that simple robust combinations like median have performed well, but we haven't tested a broad weighted combination over the full pool yet. A weighted average using inverse error weighting on the full pool of models should leverage the diverse strengths of different model families (ARIMA for trend/seasonality, ETs/THETA for level, RF/Catboost for non-linear patterns) while down-weighting outliers, potentially beating the median in terms of RMSE if the errors are somewhat correlated but not perfectly.

The current leader (median) benefits from robustness against the unstable ranking (trend_dominated regime). To challenge this, I will test a simple unweighted mean over the full pool, which serves as a baseline for how much benefit is gained from explicit weighting vs. raw averaging in this noisy environment.

This reduces noise from the correlated lower-tier models.
